passage:
Editor's note on Shalini's first month, Tuesday
Shalini, our new research writer, handed in her piece on the town's water supply with something I rarely see: every paragraph marked in the margin. "S" for things she saw herself at the pumping station. "T" for things officials told her. "G" for her own guesses, in a different colour.
Irfan, who has been here for years, had written that the pipes were "forty years old". Shalini asked him, "How do we know that?" He laughed, checked, and found it came from a remark at a tea stall. The records said twenty-eight.
She isn't slow; she is careful. I've asked her to show the team her margin method at Friday's meeting.
Abhinav

qa.q: What did the records say about the age of the pipes?
qa.a: The records said twenty-eight.

qa.q: Why might Shalini mark every paragraph in the margin?
qa.a: Shalini seems careful and cautious, wanting to know where each fact came from so she can keep what she saw apart from what she was told or guessed.

qa.q: What turning point shows Shalini's method working?
qa.a: Her question "How do we know that?" led Irfan to find the forty-year claim came from a tea-stall remark, and the records corrected it.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel about being checked by a new colleague?
qa.a: Irfan laughed and checked, so he seems to take it well, though he may feel a little embarrassed that a tea-stall remark slipped in.

grounding: It shows a careful young writer who marks the source of every claim and asks how a fact is known.

passage:
Thursday, 10 pm
Long day at the transport office. Jatin was sure the new bus route cut travel time by half. "Everyone's saying it," he said. I asked, "How do we know?" He rolled his eyes and called me "Madam Footnote" again.
But I tried my own trick on myself tonight. For the report I made three columns: what I saw (I rode the route twice, 42 and 47 minutes), what I was told (drivers say "much faster"), and what I'm guessing (maybe fewer stops?). The old route data says 55 minutes. So: faster, yes. Half? No.
A year ago I'd have written "half" too, because it sounded right. I'll show Jatin the draft tomorrow and let the columns do the arguing.
Amandeep

qa.q: How long did the new route take when Amandeep rode it?
qa.a: Amandeep rode the route twice, and it took 42 and 47 minutes.

qa.q: Why might Jatin feel sure the route cut time by half?
qa.a: Jatin feels confident because "everyone's saying it", so the claim feels true through repetition, even without a source.

qa.q: What method did Amandeep use for the report?
qa.a: Three columns: what she saw, what she was told and what she's guessing, then a check against the old route data.

qa.q: How might the drivers who say the route is "much faster" see Amandeep's findings?
qa.a: The drivers may feel their sense that the route is faster was fair, since the rides took 42 and 47 minutes against 55, even though the time was not cut by half.

grounding: It shows a careful young worker who separates what she saw, heard and guessed before trusting a claim.

passage:
Late at night, Nikita, a junior analyst, is finishing a market report when her teammate Gautam messages.
Gautam: can you add that 70% of customers prefer the new pack?
Nikita: where's the 70% from?
Gautam: pretty sure it was in the meeting
Nikita: I was in the meeting. Rao sir said "most people I spoke to" 🤔
Gautam: ok so 70ish?
Nikita: that's a guess. my notes have 3 labels: saw (survey data), told (meeting comments), inferred (my own reading)
Nikita: survey says 58%, out of 200
Gautam: huh. I'd have sworn 70
Nikita: happens to me too. that's why I label everything 😅
Gautam: fine, 58 with the source. you saved us a very awkward client call 🙏

qa.q: What does the survey say?
qa.a: The survey says 58%, out of 200.

qa.q: Why was Gautam so sure about 70%?
qa.a: Gautam remembered a strong impression from the meeting, where "most people" was said, and it turned into a number that felt certain.

qa.q: Which of Nikita's habits caught the error?
qa.a: Asking "where's the 70% from?" and labelling notes as saw, told and inferred, so a meeting comment could not pass as survey data.

qa.q: How might the client have reacted if the 70% had gone in?
qa.a: The client might have planned around a wrong figure and lost trust in the team once the survey was checked.

grounding: It shows a careful young analyst who asks where a claim comes from and keeps what she saw, was told and inferred apart.

passage: Revathi had been a field officer at the dairy cooperative in Kallakurichi for eight months, and her notebook had three columns: Saw, Told, Guessed. Milk collection had dropped a fifth in a month. At the tea stall Karthik said, "Fodder price doubled. Everyone knows." Revathi wrote it under Told. "Who told you, Karthik?" "Asif's cousin." Under Saw she had written: empty cans at the Pudupalayam and Melur centres, two cows in one shed looking thin. Under Guessed: maybe drought, maybe fodder. Next morning she rode her scooter to the fodder shop and copied its price board. It had risen, but by a sixth, not double. Asif added that three farmers had sold cows before a wedding season. Her report kept the columns apart, so the office could see which facts were checked.

qa.q: What were the three columns in Revathi's notebook?
qa.a: Saw, Told and Guessed.

qa.q: How did Revathi feel about Karthik's claim, and what shows it?
qa.a: Revathi felt cautious about it, writing it under Told and asking who had told Karthik, because tea-stall talk is not the same as something she has checked herself.

qa.q: What small step turned a rumour into a checked fact in Revathi's work?
qa.a: Riding to the fodder shop and copying its price board, which showed the price had risen by a sixth, not doubled.

qa.q: How might the cooperative office see Revathi's report differently from a report based only on tea-stall talk?
qa.a: The office could trust which parts were checked and which were guesses, so it could act on the real causes instead of a rumour.

grounding: The passage shows a careful worker keeping what she saw, heard and inferred separate and checking a claim before reporting it.

passage: Nadia's desk at the Salford community library was edged with sticky notes: green for something she had read in a document, yellow for something a person had told her, pink for her own guesses. She was writing a leaflet on the old cotton mill. "It shut in 1962 because of the big fire," said Gabriel, a retired volunteer, pouring tea. "My grandad was there." Nadia smiled and wrote it on yellow. "How do we know about the fire part?" "Grandad always said so." That afternoon she found the council minutes in the archive: the mill closed in 1962 after orders fell, and a fire was recorded in 1958. She showed Gabriel. He rubbed his chin. "So he joined the two stories together. Fair enough." The leaflet listed both dates, each with its source.

qa.q: What did the council minutes say about the mill?
qa.a: The mill closed in 1962 after orders fell, and a fire was recorded in 1958.

qa.q: What does Nadia's quiet smile and yellow note suggest she was thinking?
qa.a: She respected Gabriel's family story but saw it as something told, not yet checked, so she wanted to find out how solid the fire part was.

qa.q: Which step settled the question of the fire, and what did it allow?
qa.a: Looking up the council minutes in the archive; they showed the closure and the fire were four years apart, so the leaflet could list both with their sources.

qa.q: How might Gabriel feel about his grandad's story after seeing the minutes?
qa.a: He seemed to take it calmly, understanding that his grandad had joined two true events into one story rather than lying.

grounding: The passage shows a careful worker sorting what she read, was told and guessed, and checking a told claim against records.

passage: At the market research firm in Kolkata, the Monday meeting began with Harish announcing, "The client is unhappy with our last report." Heads dropped. Bidisha, a junior analyst, opened her notebook, where she kept three columns for every project: Saw, Told, Guessed. "Can I ask how we know?" she said. "Did they say it in writing?" Harish hesitated. "Not exactly. Their manager didn't smile on the call, and someone in sales heard they might switch firms." Bidisha wrote: Saw: no smile. Told: second-hand sales rumour. Guessed: unhappy. "So it's possible," she said, "but it's mostly guesswork. Should we just ask them?" Harish emailed the client. The reply came by lunch: they were happy, just busy, and wanted a follow-up study.

qa.q: What three columns does Bidisha keep for every project?
qa.a: Saw, Told, Guessed.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha feel it was worth asking 'how we know'?
qa.a: Bidisha felt cautious, suspecting the gloom came from guesses and second-hand talk rather than anything the client actually said.

qa.q: Which of Bidisha's habits made the meeting go better?
qa.a: Sorting the claim into what was seen, told and guessed, and suggesting they simply ask the client.

qa.q: How might Harish feel when the client's reply came?
qa.a: Harish would likely feel relieved and a little sheepish, since the worry had been mostly guesswork.

grounding: Shows a young analyst separating what was seen, told and inferred before accepting a claim, and checking the source.

passage:
Hi Saurabh,
Thanks for the draft report on the flood-relief camps. Before it goes to the district office, I've added a small note beside each claim about how we know it, because I've been burned before by my own memory.
'Three camps have no clean water': I saw this myself on Tuesday at Camps 2 and 5. Camp 7 I only heard about from a volunteer, so I've marked it 'reported, not checked'.
'Children are missing school': the headteacher told us; I've added her name and the date.
'Food will run out by Friday': this is our inference from the stock sheets, so I've labelled it an estimate.
I know it slows us down. But if the district officer asks 'how do you know?', we'll have an answer for every line. Could you check the Camp 7 claim tomorrow?
Lakshmi

qa.q: At which camps did Lakshmi personally see no clean water?
qa.a: At Camps 2 and 5.

qa.q: Why does Lakshmi take the trouble to label every claim?
qa.a: Lakshmi feels cautious, having been burned before by memory, and wants every line to have a clear source.

qa.q: How do Lakshmi's labels make the report stronger?
qa.a: They separate what was seen, what was told and what was inferred, so the district officer can trust each claim and see which ones need checking.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel about being asked to check the Camp 7 claim?
qa.a: Saurabh may feel the extra work is a nuisance at first, but worth it for a report that holds up.

grounding: Shows a young worker noting how each claim is known, separating what was seen, told and inferred.

passage: You asked, Vandana, why my notebooks look so strange. Every line has a little letter in the margin. I'm Alka, and I collect oral histories in the villages around Bhuj. In my first year, I wrote up a story about a well that saved a whole village in the great drought. I was sure an old man had told me he had seen it. When my editor asked for his name, I went back to my notes and found nothing. I had heard it from three different people, each of whom had heard it from someone else. None of them had seen it. That scared me. So now: S means I saw it, T means I was told it, and by whom, I means I'm inferring. Before I write any sentence, I ask myself: how do I actually know this? It's slow. It's also why people trust my work.

qa.q: What do the letters S, T and I mean in Alka's notebook?
qa.a: S means seen, T means told (and by whom), and I means inferred.

qa.q: Why did the well story scare Alka?
qa.a: Alka felt shaken on finding that a story believed to come from an eyewitness had only been passed along by people who hadn't seen it.

qa.q: What question does Alka ask before writing, and why does it help?
qa.a: 'How do I actually know this?', which separates what was seen, told and inferred before anything is written as fact.

qa.q: Why does the editor matter to the story?
qa.a: The editor's request for the old man's name made Alka check the notes and discover the gap.

grounding: Shows a young researcher marking every note by its source and asking how each claim is known.

passage:
I sit next to Vasudha at the research office, and there's something she does that I've started to copy.

Last week our manager Sudha asked whether a new method would save time. Most of us said, "Yes, everyone says it works." Vasudha paused. Then she took out her notebook and read aloud, "I saw it tested once, in our trial. I read it in two reports, but both from the same company. And I'm guessing it will help with our work, but that's my guess."

Sudha looked impressed. "So we know less than we thought."

I don't know exactly how Vasudha thinks through things. But she writes the source next to everything she reads, and she always says which part she saw herself.

qa.q: What did Vasudha read aloud from her notebook?
qa.a: That she saw it tested once, read it in two reports from the same company, and was guessing it would help.

qa.q: What does Vasudha's pause before answering suggest about her?
qa.a: It suggests she felt cautious and responsible, not wanting to claim more than she really knew.

qa.q: What habit of Vasudha's could the rest of the team adopt?
qa.a: Writing the source next to everything they read, and saying which parts they saw, were told or guessed.

qa.q: How did Sudha react to Vasudha's answer?
qa.a: Sudha looked impressed and realised the team knew less than they thought.

grounding: A colleague observes a careful worker who notes sources and separates what she saw, was told and inferred.

passage:
Monday. Ritu, a junior journalist, was writing about a factory closure. Her editor Gargi asked, "How do you know workers weren't paid?" Ritu said, "Everyone knows." Gargi raised an eyebrow.

Wednesday. Ritu went back through her notes. She split them into three columns: what she saw (locked gates, a notice), what she was told (two workers said they weren't paid), and what she guessed (the owner had money trouble).

Friday. She rewrote the article. "Two workers said they had not been paid," not "workers weren't paid." Gargi read it and nodded. "Now it's something we can stand behind." Ritu felt steadier, and kept the three columns in her notebook.

qa.q: What did Ritu put in the column for what she saw?
qa.a: Locked gates and a notice.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel after rewriting the article?
qa.a: She felt steadier and more confident, knowing each claim had a clear source.

qa.q: Why was Ritu's three-column method useful?
qa.a: It separated what she saw, was told and guessed, so her article only claimed what she could stand behind.

qa.q: How might Gargi see Ritu's change between Monday and Friday?
qa.a: Gargi seems satisfied and approving, pleased that Ritu now checks how she knows things.

grounding: A careful worker learns to note sources and separate what she saw, was told and inferred.

passage:
Amandeep, you asked how I became a good researcher. Let your Kalyani aunty tell you. When I was twenty-five, I worked at a library in Pune helping scholars.

One day a professor asked me where a certain fact came from. I said confidently, "It's in the old census." I'd read it somewhere, I was sure. But when I looked, it wasn't in the census at all. It was in a magazine article that quoted someone quoting the census, wrongly.

I felt so foolish. After that, I kept small cards for every fact I read, with the book and page. And before I told anyone anything, I asked myself: did I see this, was I told it, or did I work it out?

qa.q: Where did young Kalyani work at twenty-five?
qa.a: At a library in Pune helping scholars.

qa.q: How did young Kalyani feel when she found the fact wasn't in the census?
qa.a: Young Kalyani felt foolish, having been so confident about where it came from.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Kalyani worked with facts?
qa.a: Finding the fact came from a magazine quoting someone else made her start keeping source cards and asking how she knew each fact.

qa.q: How might the professor have felt about Kalyani's first answer?
qa.a: The professor probably trusted her answer at first, and may have been grateful when she checked and corrected it.

grounding: An elder recalls learning to note sources and ask whether she saw, was told or inferred each fact.

passage: Twenty minutes to deadline, and the newsroom was roaring. Saurabh, the desk editor, leaned over Gurpreet's screen. "Just write that the factory dumped waste in the canal. Everyone in the village says so." Gurpreet's notebook lay open. On the first day she had drawn three columns: Saw, Told, Guessed. Under Saw: brown foam near the outlet pipe, photographed at 7 a.m. Under Told: two farmers said the factory ran pumps at night. Under Guessed: that the foam came from the factory. "I saw foam at the pipe," she said. "I was told about the night pumping. I can't yet say who dumped what." Saurabh groaned, then read her columns. "Fine. Write exactly that." The story went out on time, careful and true.

qa.q: What were the three columns in Gurpreet's notebook?
qa.a: Saw, Told, Guessed.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet have been feeling when Saurabh pushed her?
qa.a: She was probably tense with the deadline, but steady and confident, because her notes showed exactly what she knew and how she knew it.

qa.q: What made Gurpreet's method work under pressure?
qa.a: Separating what she saw, what she was told and what she guessed let her state only what was supported, quickly.

qa.q: How does Saurabh's view change after reading the columns?
qa.a: Saurabh moves from impatience to trust, seeing that the story can be fair and still meet the deadline.

grounding: A careful worker separates what she saw, was told and guessed, even under deadline pressure.

passage: At her desk in the Chennai office, Sangeeta read the city's report on street lights with a pencil in hand, writing a small source tag beside every claim she copied: "p.14, city report", "Jeevan, phone call", "my guess". Jeevan rolled his chair over. "Put in that half the lights on our road are broken. I'm sure of it." "How do you know?" she asked, not unkindly. He paused. "I walk there every night. Well, I saw maybe six dark ones. And my neighbour said it's half." Sangeeta wrote: "Six dark lights seen by Jeevan; neighbour estimates half." Jeevan laughed. "You make everything sound so boring." "Boring and right," she said, "beats exciting and wrong."

qa.q: How many dark lights had Jeevan actually seen?
qa.a: Maybe six.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan feel so sure half the lights were broken?
qa.a: He walks there every night and his neighbour said so; blending what he saw with what he heard made him feel certain, and he seemed amused rather than offended when she checked.

qa.q: What could any colleague learn from Sangeeta's source tags?
qa.a: Write a short source beside each claim, such as "report", "phone call" or "my guess", and ask "how do you know?" before stating it.

qa.q: What would change if Sangeeta simply wrote that half the lights were broken?
qa.a: A neighbour's estimate would appear as fact, and anyone relying on the report could be misled.

grounding: A careful worker tags every claim with its source and asks how a colleague knows, separating what was seen from what was told.

passage:
"The stock count's fine, madam. Three hundred cartons, same as last month."
"Did you count them today, Jagdish ji?"
"Well... the loader told me this morning."
"Okay. So that's told." Jaya wrote it down. "And the register?"
"The register says three hundred."
"That's written, not seen. Did anyone see the cartons today?"
"I saw the stack. It looked the same."
"Looked the same. That's a guess from seeing, fair enough." She smiled. "Shall we count one row together? Ten minutes."
Jagdish sighed, then walked with her. Row one had forty cartons, not fifty.
"Huh," he said. "I'd have sworn."
"Me too, honestly," Jaya said. "That's why I ask how we know."

qa.q: How many cartons did row one have?
qa.a: Forty cartons, not fifty.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel when row one came up short?
qa.a: He was surprised and a bit sheepish, having been sure, because the stack looked the same and others had told him so.

qa.q: Which part of Jaya's approach made the difference?
qa.a: She sorted each claim into told, written and seen, then suggested a quick joint count, without blaming anyone.

qa.q: What would change if Jaya had simply accepted the register?
qa.a: The shortage would stay hidden and the error could grow before anyone noticed.

grounding: A careful worker asks how each claim is known, separating told, written and seen, and checks with a count.

passage:
When I joined the NGO as a research assistant last year, I thought I had a good memory. In my first report I wrote that most women in our district walk over an hour for water. Divyansh, my manager, asked, "How do you know that?" I couldn't say. A survey? A talk? A film?
Now I keep a notebook with three columns: saw, was told, worked out. On last week's village visits, "women queued at the hand pump before six" went under saw. "The pump breaks every summer" went under was told, with the name of the woman who told me. "Maybe why girls miss morning classes" went under worked out, with a question mark.
This month's report took longer. But when Divyansh asked, "How do you know?", I opened the notebook. I'm Parveen, and I trust my memory a little less and my notes a lot more.

qa.q: What are the three columns in Parveen's notebook?
qa.a: Saw, was told, worked out.

qa.q: How did Parveen feel when Divyansh first asked "How do you know that?"
qa.a: Parveen felt caught out and embarrassed, unable to say whether the claim came from a survey, a talk or a film.

qa.q: Why is the worked-out column with a question mark useful?
qa.a: It keeps a guess, like girls missing morning classes, apart from what was seen or told, so it isn't reported as fact.

qa.q: How might Divyansh see Parveen's reports now?
qa.a: Divyansh can trust them more, since each claim can be traced to something seen, told or worked out.

grounding: Shows a careful worker noting sources and keeping what was seen, what was told and what was worked out apart.
